'''''Buglossoides arvensis''''' (syn. ''Lithospermum arvense''), known as '''field gromwell''', '''corn gromwell''', '''bastard alkanet''', and '''stone seed''', is a flowering plant of the family [[Boraginaceae]]. It is native to Europe and Asia, as far north as Korea, Japan and Russia, and as far south as Afghanistan and northern Pakistan.<ref name = foc>''[http://www.efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200019085 "Lithospermum arvense Linnaeus, Sp. Pl. 1: 132. 1753".] Flora of China.''</ref> It is known in other places as an [[introduced species]], including much of North America and Australia.<ref name = usda>[https://plants.usda.gov/ '''^''' USDA Plants Profile]</ref><ref name = apni>[https://www.anbg.gov.au/cgi-bin/apni?TAXON_NAME=Buglossoides+arvensis '''^''' ''"Buglossoides arvensis".''] ''[[Australian Plant Name Index]] (APNI), IBIS database. Centre for Plant Biodiversity Research, Australian Government, Canberra. Retrieved 20 March 2012.''</ref>

==Subspecies==
Three subspecies are accepted.<ref name = powo/>
*''Buglossoides arvensis'' subsp. ''arvensis''
*''Buglossoides arvensis'' subsp. ''occidentalis'' {{small|Franco}}
*''Buglossoides arvensis'' subsp. ''sibthorpiana'' {{small|(Griseb.) R.Fern.}}

==Uses==
=== Oil ===
The European Union has granted the refined oil of the seed of ''Buglossoides arvensis'' [[novel food]] status and some farmers are growing it<ref name = Nosowitz>[[Lithospermum arvense#cite ref-4|'''^''']] ''Nosowitz, Dan (19 November 2015). [https://modernfarmer.com/2015/11/corn-gromwell-weed/ "What Is This Weird Weed, and Why Are Farmers and Health Nuts So Into It?".] [[Modern Farmer (magazine)|Modern Farmer]]. Retrieved 30 November 2015.''</ref> commercially in the United Kingdom as a plant-variety patented (PVP) and trademarked cultivar (Ahiflower®). The seed oil contains high levels (63–72%) of omega-3 ALA (c18:3), omega-3 SDA (c18:4), and omega-6 GLA (c18:3)<ref>Lefort (2016) Consumption of Buglossoides arvensis seed oil is safe and increases tissue long-chain n-3 fatty acid content more than flax seed oil. [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/26793308/ ''J Nutr Sci'' 5:e2, 1-12.] ''Retrieved 10 Jun 2022.''</ref> and has GRAS (generally regarded as safe) review status from the US Food and Drug Administration, Canadian ingredient master file (IMF) registration and novel food status, and GMP+ Feed Support Product status in the EU for livestock and companion animals (including for defatted expeller press cake meal). The seed oil also has TGA Australia Complementary Medicines approval status, ANVISA/MAPA Brazil human and animal alimentary use approval, and limited food use approvals in Korea and Japan.

Refined ''Buglossoides'' oil has peer-reviewed published human clinical evidence from controlled dietary intervention trials showing up to 400% more efficient omega-3 EPA (c20:5) accrual in circulating cells vs flaxseed oil and has been shown to significantly upregulate the cytokine interleukin-10 (IL-10) in lipopolysaccharide (LPS) stimulated macrophages by +40% vs. control.<ref>Lefort (2017) Dietary ''Buglossoides arvensis'' oil increases circulating n-3 polyunsaturated fatty acids in a dose-dependent manner and enhances lipopolysaccharide-stimulated whole blood interleukin-10—a randomized placebo-controlled trial. [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/28287415/ ''Nutrients'' 9:261; 1-17]. ''Retrieved 10 Jun 2022.''</ref> IL-10 is recognized as one of the immune modulatory signaling cytokines that moderates the inflammatory response after intensive exercise or immune challenge. Further, refined Buglossoides oil has been shown to form omega-3 DHA (C22:6) endogenously with comparable efficiency as pure marine DHA in mammals and maintain DHA levels similarly in the brain and liver.<ref>Metherel A (2021) Determining plasma and tissue DHA turnover from Ahiflower® oil, flaxseed oil and DHA using compound specific isotopic analysis. [https://aocs.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/toc/15589331/2021/98/S1 J Am Oil Chem Soc 2021];98(Suppl. 1):242–243.</ref> It has also been shown in recent peer-reviewed research to promote live probiotic survival into the small intestine in the TIMS-1 simulated gut<ref>Venema K et al. (2020) Survival of a probiotic-containing product using capsule-within-capsule technology in an in vitro model of the stomach and small intestine (TIM-1). [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32264687/ Beneficial Microbes 2020]; 11(4): 403-409</ref> and contribute beneficially to anti-neuroinflammation response in vitro<ref>Cumberford G et al. (2023) Methods and compositions with purified Bombyx morii cocoon silk fiber and refined Buglossoides arvensis seed oil providing anti-inflammatory effects and neuroprotection for disease states. [https://patents.google.com/patent/US11707497B2/en?oq=US+11707497B2+ Patent #US 11707497B2] (July 25, 2023), p. 101.</ref> and synergistically to improved executive function and cognitive flexibility in healthy adults.<ref>Lanou A (2023) A randomized, placebo-controlled clinical trial of a novel dietary supplement (Braini) on standardized CNS vital signs cognitive performance parameters in adults. [https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36856456/ J Integr Complement Med. 2023]; May;29(5):303-312.</ref> Based on its fatty acid composition, refined Buglossoides oil naturally provides the body a more diverse array of anti-inflammatory omega-3 and omega-6 (via GLA) substrates than derive from preformed EPA/DHA sources. These include SDA, ETA (C20:4n-3), GLA, and DGLA (C20:3n-6).

=== Archaeological record ===
Seeds of ''Buglossoides'' have been reported in Ukrainian archeological sites dating back as far as 4000 BC where they were stored in clay pots, however the purpose and usage of the seeds has not been determined. In modern European arable agriculture, ''Buglossoides'' often appears as a weed species with poor competitive and non-invasive characteristics.
